title: TA9-06463
frame:
Forum: Refugee Protection Division (first-instance tribunal).
Parties: the claimant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review: none; this is the first-instance decision.
How the layers nest here: The member of the tribunal is the author (layer 1). The claimant and the Minister make submissions to the member (layer 2). There is no earlier decision-maker unless the reasons describe a prior decision (layer 3). Testimony and documents are layer 5.

paragraphs.text: XXXXX XXXXX (the claimant), a citizen of the People's Republic of China (China), claims refugee protection pursuant to section 96 and subsection 97 (1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act1 (IRPA). Allegations
The claimant alleges the following.

The claimant was introduced to Christianity in XXXXX 2007 because he was sad and depressed after his grandmother's death on XXXXX 2006. The claimant hesitated when told that the house church he was about to join was illegal but was assured by his friend that they had operated many years without detection or problems. The claimant joined the underground house church on XXXXX, 2007 and continued to regularly attend and acquire Christian knowledge. The claimant was at a wedding on XXXXX 2007 when the house church was raided by the Public Security Bureau (PSB). After a warning telephone call from his friend, the claimant went into hiding. The PSB came to the claimant's house two days later, searched the house, and accused the claimant of being involved with illegal underground church activities. After learning that several of his fellow believers had been arrested, the claimant, with the help of his family, found an agent to help him leave China and come to Canada. Determination

The panel finds that the claimant is not a Convention refugee as he does not have a well-founded fear of persecution for a Convention ground in China. The panel also finds that the claimant is not a person in need of protection in that his removal to China would not subject him personally to a risk to his life or to a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment, and in that there are no substantial grounds to believe that his removal to China will subject him personally to a danger of torture. Analysis

The determinative issue in regard to this claim is the credibility of the claimant's oral testimony, Personal Information Form2 (PIF) narrative and amendments, and the Citizenship and Immigration Canada (CIC) Refugee Intake Record of Examination,3 concerning Christian membership in China and in Canada, and his pursuit by authorities in China. The panel finds, on a balance of probabilities, that the claimant is not a credible witness in this regard. Identity
The claimant's identity is established as a national of China by an original Resident Identity Card (RIC) and Hukou.4 Credibility

The claimant stated at the first sitting that he did not understand the interpreter during the intake interview with the CIC.5 He stated during testimony that he told the interviewer on one occasion that he did not understand the interpreter. The claimant stated that he asked questions to be repeated and when they were repeated, he still did not understand. The claimant was asked when he did this during the interview and he said, "I forgot". There is no mention by the CIC Immigration officer, during the interview, of any objection, statement, or indication of difficulty with the interpretation. The claimant stated that he was afraid at the time and therefore did not mention the difficulty. The claimant was asked why he came to Canada and he said because the smuggler told him to come to Canada. This testimony is not plausible. The claimant paid, according to the evidence presented, 180,000 RMB to the smuggler. One could reasonably assume that the claimant would have been given information by the smuggler about the safety, justice, and good treatment in Canada after paying such a large sum of money. The claimant left his country because he allegedly feared arrest and came to a country where he would escape that fear and yet stated that he was still afraid. The panel draws a negative inference from this testimony. It is also reasonable to assume that when being interviewed by a Canadian immigration official that the claimant would give information freely and if he did not understand the interpreter would certainly say so. For the claimant to give information when, according to testimony, he did not understand the interpreter, is not reasonable or credible.

Counsel stated in his submissions a number of examples of case law from the Federal Court of Appeal and the Federal Court of Canada stating that the process for gathering information at the Intake interview is flawed. The process may not be perfect in that this interview was conducted with the interpreter by the telephone, was not recorded and cannot be checked for accuracy in translation, and no counsel was present. The panel is also aware that during this process, the claimant could be nervous and distracted. However, the panel would reasonably expect the CIC Immigration officer to be aware of the claimant being hesitant or giving other indications that the translations were not being given accurately or understood by the claimant when the questions were being asked in his native language. By the same token, the translator, is also trained in interpreting, and would have reasonably indicated if the claimant did not understand the translations, by giving unusual answers or continually asking for questions to be repeated. The process at the CIC Intake interview may not be perfect but the panel is persuaded, because of the professionalism of the people involved, that it is an accurate recording of the claimant's testimony. The panel also believes that at this time, the issues regarding the claimant leaving China should be fresh and current and not clouded by the passage of time.

The claimant denied that he knew what passport he used when he came to Canada. He stated that his picture was in the passport but he did not know the name. The claimant did not recall telling the Canadian immigration official that his passport was from Indonesia.6 The claimant stated, in testimony, he did not say that. The panel draws a negative inference from this testimony. As stated previously, the Immigration officers and interpreters are highly qualified and would not put down a piece of information that the claimant had not given them. Counsel disagreed with the questioning at this point and it was taken under advisement. Schedule 1 of the Intake interview is an information gathering process and there is no reason for information to be recorded that was not given by the claimant. In the claimant's PIF,7 he stated that he did not know which passport was used. The panel draws a negative inference from this inconsistent testimony between the Intake interview and PIF,8 where he stated he did not know the country of origin of the passport.

The claimant was asked what he would say if he had been discovered, en route, with false documentation. The claimant said the smuggler told him to follow him. The claimant then became evasive and did not answer the question. He continued to say the smuggler said, "it was no problem and to keep behind him". The claimant stated that if he was asked his citizenship, the smuggler would answer for him. He gave the same response when he was asked what he would say if someone inquired about his name. This testimony is not plausible. It is not reasonable that the claimant could go through customs at Hong Kong, Beijing, and Canada without being asked a question regarding his identity, destination, or purpose of travel. The panel draws a negative inference from this testimony.

In the Intake interview,9 the claimant was asked to provide the routing information for his trip, and he initially said that he did not know. When asked a second time, the claimant stated that he flew from Hong Kong, Beijing to Canada. The claimant explained that he was afraid when being asked the question. For reasons stated earlier in these reasons, the panel does not accept this explanation as reasonable and draws a negative inference from this inconsistent testimony at the Intake interview. The claimant admitted in testimony that he misled the Immigration officer as to the itinerary. The claimant had a statutory obligation to tell the truth but clearly did not honour this obligation and therefore created doubt about the claimant's credibility.

The claimant stated during the Intake interview by CIC10 that he had a legally issued Chinese passport. The claimant, during testimony, said he had never been issued a passport. When reminded that he replied positively twice to that question during the CIC Intake interview, he responded by saying, "I did not say that". The claimant was reminded that he stated during his CIC Intake interview that he gave his passport to his friend to keep in a safe place.11 The claimant also answered positively during the Intake interview in answering the question, "Have you ever been issued a passport or travel document of which you are the rightful holder?" The panel draws a negative inference from this inconsistent, evasive, and evolving testimony. The panel finds, on a balance of probabilities, that the claimant, given the previous inconsistencies, negative inferences, and implausibilities, between testimony and evidence submitted, is not a credible witness. Underground Christian church in China

The claimant stated that he had not been aware of Christianity before his friend's conversations in XXXXX 2007. He first attended the underground church on XXXXX 2007 when his friend took him to the meeting. He stated that he went every week on Sundays until the Sunday before the raid XXXXX 2007 and that there were 12 members in their group. The underground house church had no overseas affiliation and he took no leadership role with the group. He stated the church had been operating for two years and did not have any problems.

The claimant was asked to list all precautions taken by the underground church. He stated there were lookouts at the front and back. He was then asked by the Tribunal Officer (TO) if there was a telephone and he responded, "Yes". He was asked if that was at the same location and he responded, "No", there were three locations. He was asked if there were front and back doors and he responded, "Yes." He was asked if the lookout's job was to make a telephone call if anything suspicious happened and the claimant said there was telecommunication of some sort. He was asked if the PSB came to the front door, would they escape from the back and vice versa and the claimant responded, "Yes". When asked if the PSB went to both doors, the claimant said the originator took away the Bibles and pretended it was a normal gathering. All of these answers above were given after prompts from the TO. The claimant was asked if there were any other precautions and he said, "No". The claimant said the church service was held at eight o'clock in the evening but did not know the reason. He stated that the organizer set the time. He did not know if the reason for the time was that there were fewer people around. When asked if it was urban or rural, he stated, "rural" and when asked, "Why", he said, "Because it was more secret." The claimant said that this should be a precaution. He was asked if they sang hymns and he replied, "No" because the singing could be heard by others and he agreed that this was another precaution. He agreed that closing the blinds was another precaution. When the claimant was asked why he did not mention these precautions earlier, he said, "Because you were asking for an escape plan." The question asked was to list all of the precautions of the underground Christian church. The panel draws a negative inference from the claimant's lack of information about the precautions taken by the underground church in case the PSB raided. The claimant gave most of his answers when prompted or given the information by the TO. Counsel stated in his submissions that the claimant's limited response was sufficient. The panel disagrees and draws a negative inference from this testimony. One would reasonably expect a person who was involved with an illegal underground activity would be aware of all precautions taken, because of the alleged risk, and be able describe these precautions in detail.

At the Canadian Border Service's Agency interview,12 the claimant stated that the PSB were trying to arrest the head of the "Christianity" underground so the brothers and sisters ran away. The claimant use the word "Christianity" twice during the interview and the immigration officer made special note. The panel finds it unreasonable that the claimant was allegedly a member of the underground church in China for some three and a half months and allegedly studied the Bible and attended services but could not identify Christianity by its proper name. Although this is not a critical issue in the decision of the claim, because of previous credibility issues, the panel draws a negative inference from this misuse of the word Christianity. The claimant also stated in this interview,13 as noted above, that they were not coming to arrest him but the head of the Christian underground. This is inconsistent with testimony in his PIF narrative and testimony where he alleges the PSB were looking for him and questioned family members. Counsel stated in his submissions that there was a declaration made by the claimant14 that negated the above inconsistency in testimony and evidence. This declaration was made by the claimant on 30, July 2007 and translated on May 7, 2009. The claimant in this declaration does not mention the head of the underground church specifically, but does mention that he heard the PSB were going after the underground church and that a few people in his church had been arrested. There was no mention of the PSB looking for him and no indication of where he heard this information. This declaration is still inconsistent with the testimony given in the claimant's PIF and does not indicate that the PSB came to the claimant's home to look for him. Although counsel believes that this declaration negates the previous information given to the CIC Immigration officer, the panel does not agree. In fact, this additional declaration raises further questions regarding the claimant's credibility. To give differing testimony on the same day at the Intake interview is not reasonable, or credible. The panel finds, on a balance of probabilities, that the claimant was never a member of the underground Christian house church. The PSB

The claimant stated that the PSB came to visit his home on XXXXX, 2007 and during that visit, they accused him of being involved in illegal underground house church religious activities. He stated that the PSB searched his home and questioned his family members. The PSB allegedly came back one week later and have continued to visit his home in China continuously. The last visit by the PSB, according to the claimant, was XXXXX 2009. The claimant stated that no documents were ever produced in spite of the alleged search of his home and potential arrest of the claimant. The panel draws a negative inference with respect to the claimant's credibility due to the lack of summons left by the PSB. The claimant alleges that the PSB are pursuing him and have made repeated attempts to find him. The claimant also says that despite all of this, no summons was ever left for him. It was submitted by Counsel, with reference to the country documentary evidence15 that leaving a summons with family is not a proper procedure. However, the same document provides that, according to the representative of Human Rights in China in New York,16 ... it is very common in China for the police authorities to leave a summons or subpoena with family members (or possibly close friends, though that is probably less common), instructing them to pass it along to the person named on the summons. The person accepting the summons would be expected to sign an acknowledgment of receipt. This is not actually the proper procedure, but it happens all the time, especially in cases when the person on the summons is not easily locatable... [S]ome police officers themselves are not well versed in the proper procedures, and probably think that this is a perfectly acceptable practice...

The panel cannot help but question the genuine interest of the PSB in the claimant. Country document evidence17 indicates that it is common that a summons is left with or shown to family members when the police want someone to come to their headquarters. Although this policy is not always implemented, it is reasonable that one would have been issued in respect of the claimant given that the claimant testified that the PSB had gone to his home continuously in search of him. In addition, the summons is the documentary basis for the subsequent issuance of an arrest warrant if the person in whom they are interested does not respond to the summons. The panel finds, on a balance of probabilities, that the claimant was never wanted by the PSB for his alleged membership in an illegal underground church. Christianity

The claimant said he found the Pentecostal church that he is attending in Toronto by asking some people in Chinatown. The pastor's letter indicates that he asked some Christian questions of the claimant when he first attended the church. The claimant was asked what these questions were but did not respond to the question. Instead, he answered that he will attend Bible study and baptism classes. When the claimant was asked what his faith means to him, he stated that he will go to heaven and would have eternal life. When prompted for additional information, the claimant hesitated and then said, "Love others like loving self, love enemies, have love for God and believing Jesus." When asked what his central Christian beliefs were, he began to say, "Only son of God, born by Virgin Mary, died under Pontius Pilate." The claimant was told that this sounded like he was reading the Apostles Creed. The claimant was unable to articulate his central beliefs concerning Christianity.

The claimant recited the Lord's Prayer and Psalm 23 accurately. The claimant stated that Christmas was the first holiday that he celebrated in Canada and that holiday commemorated Lord Jesus' birth. When asked why this was significant, the claimant stated because he had never experienced the images in China that he saw in Canada and that he was baptized on that day. The claimant knew that John the Baptist baptized Jesus and that baptism washed away a person's sins. The claimant understood that Good Friday celebrated the Lord Jesus dying for us and that his resurrection three days later was commemorated by Easter. He stated that Jesus shed his blood for our redemption.

The claimant understood the purpose of the sacraments of communion and baptism. When the claimant was asked to talk about Jesus, he stated that his first miracle was the changing of water into wine because the host ran out of wine at a wedding. He correctly named three prophets in the Old Testament. The claimant was asked when and to whom Jesus appeared after crucifixion. The claimant stated the first time Jesus appeared was to Maria but did not know any other times that Jesus appeared. He said he forgot.

The claimant answered counsel's questions regarding Christianity, correctly stating that Jesus was baptized in the River Jordan by John, Judas betrayed Jesus for 30 coins and then hung himself, the role of the Holy Spirit in telling good from bad, how hallelujah means praising God, and that somebody filled with the Holy Spirit can speak in tongues or dialect.

The claimant belongs to the Pentecostal church in Toronto. When asked about the Pentecost, the claimant did not have much information. The claimant has been in Canada since July 27, 2007 and would have had the opportunity, in that he attends church every Sunday according to testimony, to experience the celebration of Pentecost at his church at least twice. This holiday is one of the major holidays celebrated in the Pentecostal church. The panel draws a negative inference from the claimant's lack of knowledge about one of the major holidays of his church. The claimant was asked to give a testimonial, again one of the major celebrations in the Pentecostal church. The claimant said that the pastor prayed for him. He said that he fell asleep and when he woke up, the pastor asked him what he dreamed about and the claimant told him he saw a white light and the pastor explained that it could have been God. A testimonial in the Pentecostal church is when a member of the congregation who has had difficulty and received assistance from God in solving the problem, stands in front of the congregation and tells his story and how God helped him solve the problem. The panel draws a negative inference from the claimant's lack of knowledge about a major ceremony in the Pentecostal church. One could reasonably expect over a period of approximately two and half years that the claimant, who has been attending a Pentecostal church, would have seen and heard many testimonials.

The claimant has an adequate knowledge of Christianity, knowledge that could be learned by reading the Bible. The panel does not expect perfect knowledge after two and a half years of attendance in the Pentecostal church in Canada. However, the panel has concerns that the claimant did not know the celebration of a major holiday in his home church and had no information about a major ceremony in the Pentecostal church, a testimonial. The claimant also could not articulate how he celebrated his faith.

The claimant has presented documentation to indicate his attendance at a Pentecostal church in Canada; a pastor's letter, a certificate of baptism, and pictures of his baptism.18 These documents indicate the claimant's attendance at the Pentecostal church but not the genuineness of his faith. The panel finds that the claimant has acquired some knowledge about Christianity but as expressed earlier, has concerns over the claimant's lack of knowledge about regular celebratory functions in the Pentecostal church that he attends. The other concern expressed by the panel is the claimant's avoidance in answering the question, "What questions were you asked by the pastor to assess your Christian knowledge?" The panel finds, on a balance of probabilities, that the claimant is not a genuine practicing Christian in the Pentecostal church in Canada.

There is a requirement for 'good faith' in making a refugee claim. In this regard, R.P.G. Haines, the Chairman of a Refugee Status Appeal Panel and A.G. Wang Heed, a member of the United Nations High Commission for Refugees stated in part: If there is no good faith requirement in the sur place situation, it places in the hands of the appellant for refugee status the means of unilaterally determining the grant to him or her of refugee status.19

In this regard, the panel cites the following from James Hathaway's The Law of Refugee Status with regard to "sur place" claims: An individual who as a stratagem deliberately manipulates circumstances to create a real chance of persecution which did not exist cannot be said to belong to this category.20
The panel finds, on a balance of probabilities, that this claim has not been made in good faith.

The panel has considered whether there is a serious possibility that the claimant would be persecuted if he returns to China and practices Christianity with the knowledge he has acquired in Canada. The claimant is from Fujian province and has lived and worked there all of his life. The panel notes the documentary evidence states: ...the Executive Secretary of the Hong Kong Christian Council commented that Fujian and Guangdong have "the most liberal policy on religion in China, especially on Christianity" (Executive Secretary 1 Sept. 2005a). In his travels, the Executive Secretary has met with local authorities who, he said, usually tolerate activities of unregistered Christian groups (ibid.). While authorities are of a more tolerant nature in rural areas than in urban centres, they would usually take steps to discourage religious activity if it had a link to groups from outside China (ibid.). The Executive Secretary stated that he is aware of a number of unregistered churches that have been allowed to function for years (ibid.). Though he has received a few reports of arrests of Catholic priests in the years 2003 to 2005, the Executive Secretary noted that overall, Christians in Fujian and Guangdong "enjoy one of the most liberal polic[ies] on religious freedom in China." (ibid.).21

The panel also notes that though there were arrests of Christians documented in 2005, 2006, 2007 and 2008, none of these arrests were noted as being in Fujian Province. In 2005, there were reports of house church crackdowns in the provinces of Shanxi, Henan, Hubei, Jiangxi, and Jilin and in May 2005, Chinese officials coordinated raids on 100 house churches in Jilin Province [northeast China], arresting approximately 600 Christians.22 During the year, there were also reports of similar incidents in Hebei, Xinjiang, Beijing and Shanghai.23 The United States 2008 International Religious Freedom Report24 specifically reviews arrests of Christians in China in 2006 and 2007 and notes arrests of Christians in Beijing, Shandong Province, Xinjiang Province, Liaoning Province, Henan province, Jiangsu province, Anhui Province, Zhejiang Province, Szechuan Province, Jiangxi Province, Hebei Province, Guanguxi Province, and Shaanxi Province. No mention is made of arrests of Christians in Fujian province in 2006 and 2007. The panel has reviewed the most recent articles25 in the exhibits covering 2008 and 2009 and have noted arrests of Christians in Beijing, Xinjiang Province, Guizhou Province, Hubei Province, and Henan Province, but none in Fujian Province. The Annual Report of the United States Commission on International Religious Freedom26 states that "arrests for and harassment of peaceful Protestant religious activity occurred in at least 17 provinces and two municipalities with the most incidents occurring in Henan, Xinjiang, Shandong, Hebei and Zhejiang provinces. The panel has reviewed all the documentary evidence submitted and the panel has found no recent evidence of arrests of Protestant Christians in Fujian Province.

The Annual Report of Persecution by the Government on Christian Churches within Mainland China27 very specifically notes the arrests and incidents of persecution of Christians in China from January 2007 to December 2007, and none of these incidents occurred in Fujian province where the claimant is from. This report states that during 2007, the number of Christians persecuted in all of China was 788 and that the number of Christians arrested and detained was 693, of which 415 were church leaders, which accounts for 59.9% of all people arrested and 52.6% of all people persecuted. The panel has reviewed all the documentary evidence submitted and the only mention of arrests of lay Christians in Fujian province was in 2002 when 20 unregistered Catholics were arrested while attending Catechism classes.28

The panel has considered all of the documents submitted about the situation for Christians in China, specifically the articles and reports documenting arrests and persecution. The panel finds, on a balance of probabilities, that if there were arrests of lay Christians in Fujian Province after 2002, there would be some documentation of these arrests. As well, the panel has considered that the China Aid Association (CAA) has stated in its report and letters that they have not documented all cases of persecution. However, the panel notes again that there has been no mention at all of recent arrests of lay Christians in Fujian Province in any of the documentation regarding religious persecution in China, and according to the latest United States Department of State Report,29 the extent of religious freedom in China continues to vary widely within the country. The panel finds that the situation in Fujian Province does not reflect what is happening in many other provinces where there have been arrests of ordinary Christians.

The panel has considered the claimant's testimony that he was a member of an underground church that was raided and that he is now wanted by the PSB who have continued to go to his home in China looking for him. The British Home Office Report notes that 31.4% of Chinese nationals aged sixteen and older are religious30 and that there are forty to seventy million Protestant Christians in China with only ten million practicing their religion in registered churches.31 That report also states that prayer meetings and Bible study groups held among friends and families are legal and need not register with authorities.32 The United States Department of State Report33 notes that house churches were more likely to have problems when the membership grew, arranged for regular use of facilities or forged links with other groups. There is no persuasive evidence that the claimant's alleged group did any of these things. His group remained small, and during their gatherings, they would allegedly recite and discuss Bible passages and pray. A pastor would come to the church a few times each year. The panel considered the claimant's description of his house church and considered its location in Fujian Province, where there have been no recent reported arrests of lay Christians. The panel has carefully reviewed the documentary evidence and finds, on a balance of probabilities, that the house church the claimant allegedly attended was never raided by the authorities and consequently, the claimant is not wanted by the PSB. The panel therefore finds, on a balance of probabilities, that the claimant would be able to continue to learn about Christianity and practice religion if he were to return to his home in Fujian Province in China and that there is not a serious possibility that he would be persecuted for doing so.

On the basis of the totality of the evidence and the cumulative findings, the panel finds that the claimant has not satisfied his burden of establishing a serious possibility that he would be persecuted or that he would be personally subjected to a risk to his life or a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment or a danger of torture by any authority in the People's Republic of China. Counsel's submissions were taken into account when writing these reasons.

The panel finds that the claimant is not a Convention refugee as he does not have a well-founded fear of persecution for a Convention ground in China. The panel also finds that the claimant is not a person in need of protection in that his removal to China would not subject him personally to a risk to his life or to a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment, and in that there are no substantial grounds to believe that his removal to China will subject him personally to a danger of torture. Conclusion

The claimant is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection. The Refugee Protection Division therefore rejects his claim. (signed) "R.S. Garner" R.S.
